passage: The lights went out in the middle of the chemistry practical, and the lab fell into grey afternoon gloom. Jomon kept working by the window, counting drops carefully, and finished his titration first. His readings were neat, three trials within a whisker of each other. Mr Pillai walked past without looking at the sheet. Two minutes later Jomon knocked a stool with his foot. "Of course. Jomon again," Mr Pillai said. "Our naughty champion since Class 8." A few students laughed. Avni, at the next bench, leaned over. "Your numbers are better than mine," she whispered. Jomon shrugged and turned the sheet face down. On the bus home he didn't open his notebook at all. What was the point of trying, he thought, if only the stool got noticed?

qa.q: What did Mr Pillai say when Jomon knocked a stool?
qa.a: Mr Pillai said, 'Of course. Jomon again,' and called him 'our naughty champion since Class 8.'

qa.q: What is Jomon thinking on the bus home?
qa.a: Jomon feels discouraged and unseen, wondering what the point of trying is if only the stool gets noticed. 😔

qa.q: How could Mr Pillai handle the next practical better?
qa.a: He could look at every sheet before commenting and name Jomon's neat readings as clearly as he names his slips.

qa.q: How does Avni see Jomon's work compared with the teacher?
qa.a: Avni actually looks at his sheet and sees his numbers are better than hers, while Mr Pillai only noticed the stool.

grounding: A teacher's old 'naughty' label means a boy's careful practical goes unseen while one clumsy slip is called out.

passage: Amandeep had rewritten his Hindi essay twice, once at the dining table and once on the balcony of their Pune flat while the pressure cooker whistled. He handed it in on Monday, a day early. On Thursday the essays came back. Mrs Rao read three aloud and praised their opening lines. Amandeep's had a big tick and nothing else. Then, when his phone buzzed in his bag during the last period, she stopped the class. "Some people never change," she said, looking straight at him. "Trouble from day one." Chandrika turned around and mouthed, "Yours was good, I read it." Amandeep nodded, but his ears were hot. At home he pushed the essay into the back of a drawer without showing anyone.

qa.q: When did Amandeep hand in his Hindi essay?
qa.a: He handed it in on Monday, a day early.

qa.q: What do Amandeep's hot ears and hidden essay suggest he feels?
qa.a: They suggest he feels embarrassed and unseen, since his careful essay got only a tick while one buzzing phone drew a public comment.

qa.q: What could Amandeep do so his effort gets seen?
qa.a: He could show the essay to someone at home, or ask Mrs Rao privately for feedback on it, so the work is looked at apart from the label.

qa.q: What would change if Mrs Rao read Amandeep's essay without her old picture of him?
qa.a: She might notice the rewriting, praise it like the others, and treat the buzzing phone as a small slip rather than proof.

grounding: A teacher who sees a boy as 'trouble' skips his careful essay but spotlights a single slip in front of the class.

passage:
In Class 9, our maths teacher called me "the sleepy one" in the first week, because I yawned during the register. I'm Thomas, and that name followed me for a year.
When I finished a whole page of algebra, she said, "Someone must have helped the sleepy boy." When I forgot my compass once, the whole class heard about it. My friend Noor once swapped our notebooks as an experiment. Same answers, my handwriting copied by Noor. Noor's version got "Excellent." Mine, the week before, got "Late again?"
I stopped raising my hand. What was the point? It felt like she was only looking for the mistakes.
It changed in Class 10, with a new teacher who didn't know the name. By December I was answering again.

qa.q: What did the maths teacher call Thomas in the first week?
qa.a: She called him "the sleepy one".

qa.q: How did the label make Thomas feel, and what did it lead him to do?
qa.a: He felt discouraged and unfairly judged, as if his good work would never be noticed and she was only looking for mistakes, so he stopped raising his hand.

qa.q: What change turned things around for Thomas, and why did it help?
qa.a: A new teacher in Class 10 who didn't know the name judged his work fresh, so he felt seen again and started answering by December.

qa.q: How might Noor see the notebook experiment?
qa.a: Noor probably found it unfair and a little shocking that the same answers got 'Excellent' for Noor and 'Late again?' for Thomas, and may have wanted to prove it to Thomas.

grounding: A teenage boy labelled early as sleepy finds his good work ignored and small slips noticed, showing how a label limits what others see.

passage:
Counsellor's note, Ankita, St. Joseph's Higher Secondary, Wednesday.
Francis, Class 10, came in at lunch, not in trouble this time. He'd been sent twice last year for being "naughty" and I think that word has stayed on him. He showed me his science notebook: a full, neat experiment write-up with no remark at all. On the next page, one ink smudge, circled in red: "Careless as usual."
"Ma'am, I did the whole thing properly," he said quietly. "No one reads it. They just look for what I did wrong." He kept pressing his thumb into the notebook's edge.
I asked him what would help. He wanted one teacher to see his work without the old story attached.
What I did next: with Francis's permission, I spoke to his science teacher today. We agreed she would give feedback on his next two write-ups using his roll number only, without his name.

qa.q: What was circled in red on the next page of Francis's notebook?
qa.a: One ink smudge, circled in red: "Careless as usual."

qa.q: What does Francis pressing his thumb into the notebook edge suggest he was feeling?
qa.a: It suggests he felt tense and let down, hurt that his proper work went unread while any small slip was picked out.

qa.q: What did Ankita do after listening, and why might it help?
qa.a: With his permission Ankita spoke to his science teacher, who agreed to mark his next two write-ups by roll number only, so his work could be judged without the old label.

qa.q: If you were the science teacher, what might you notice when marking by roll number?
qa.a: The teacher might discover that the neat, careful write-ups belong to Francis, and realise the 'naughty' label had been colouring what they saw.

grounding: A counsellor's note shows a teenage boy whose earlier label means his good work is ignored while small slips are noticed.

passage:
Monday. In the first week of Class 9, Amandeep fell asleep in the last period after a night of helping at his father's dhaba. Jahnavi ma'am woke him in front of everyone. "Our lazy Amandeep," she said, and the class laughed. The name stuck.
Wednesday. Amandeep handed in the history project two days early, with maps he had drawn by hand. Ma'am took it without a word. That afternoon he forgot his geometry box, and she said loudly, "Of course. Lazy Amandeep." He stared at his desk, face burning.
Friday. The projects came back. His had a B and one line: "Neat, but late effort as usual." It had not been late. Amandeep turned the page over so nobody could see, and didn't raise his hand once all day, even when he knew the answer.

qa.q: What did Amandeep draw by hand for the history project?
qa.a: Maps.

qa.q: How did Amandeep feel when his project came back?
qa.a: He felt hurt and defeated, because his early, careful work was called late, as if the label mattered more than what he actually did.

qa.q: What could the teacher do to see Amandeep fairly?
qa.a: Check the facts, like the early submission, look at each piece of work on its own, and ask why he was so tired that first week.

qa.q: What might change if Jahnavi ma'am had asked why Amandeep was sleepy?
qa.a: She would learn he had been helping at his father's dhaba, and the lazy label might never have started.

grounding: Over a week, a boy labelled lazy by a teacher finds his early, careful work ignored while every small slip is pointed out.

passage: Sahil, you think your teacher has decided you're a troublemaker and nothing will change it? Let your Sumit chacha tell you what happened to me at fourteen. In Class 8 I threw a paper ball once, just once, and it hit Mr Bhalla. From that day I was "the naughty one." If anyone talked, he looked at me. When I won the inter-house quiz, he said, "Even naughty boys get lucky." When I forgot my tie, it was "typical." I stopped trying. Why bother? Then in Class 10 a new teacher, Mrs Dsouza, arrived. She didn't know the label. She read my essay out loud and said, "Who wrote this? It's excellent." The whole class turned to look at me. I'll never forget how strange it felt to be seen.

qa.q: What did Mr Bhalla say when young Sumit won the quiz?
qa.a: "Even naughty boys get lucky."

qa.q: Why did young Sumit stop trying in Mr Bhalla's class?
qa.a: He felt hopeless and unfairly judged, because his wins were called luck and every small slip was called typical.

qa.q: What was the turning point in Sumit's story, and why did it matter?
qa.a: A new teacher who didn't know the label praised his essay; being judged on his actual work let him feel seen again.

qa.q: How might Mrs Dsouza have felt reading the essay aloud?
qa.a: She was probably pleased and curious, simply enjoying good writing with no label in the way.

grounding: An uncle recalls how, as a teenager labelled naughty, his wins were called luck and his slips typical, until a new teacher saw his work.

passage: The board practical was starting in ten minutes when the lab's water tap burst, spraying the benches. Bhupen, nearest, dived under the sink and shut the valve with his bare hands, soaking his shirt. When Mr Gogoi rushed in, he saw only Bhupen, dripping, next to the broken tap. "Bhupen again! Always some trouble with you." Bhupen opened his mouth, but the invigilator was already calling roll numbers, and there was no time. All through the exam he sat in a wet shirt, hands shaking, getting the titration wrong twice. Afterwards Ira, who had seen everything, went straight to Mr Gogoi. "Sir, he stopped the water. We'd have lost the whole lab." Mr Gogoi paused, then looked at Bhupen's wet shirt for a long moment.

qa.q: How did Bhupen stop the water?
qa.a: He dived under the sink and shut the valve with his bare hands.

qa.q: How did Bhupen feel sitting the exam in a wet shirt?
qa.a: He was upset and shaken, hands trembling, after being blamed for the burst tap he had actually stopped.

qa.q: What could Mr Gogoi have done differently when he rushed in?
qa.a: Ask what happened before blaming anyone, instead of letting the trouble label decide what he saw.

qa.q: How might Ira feel after telling Mr Gogoi the truth?
qa.a: Ira may feel nervous but relieved, glad to have stood up for Bhupen.

grounding: Under exam pressure, a boy with a troublemaker label is blamed for the burst tap he actually stopped.

passage: In Class 10C of the Andheri school, the physics teacher had a name for Ujjwal: "our sleeping beauty." It started in June, when he dozed off once after a late night helping at his uncle's shop. Since then, nothing he did seemed to count. On Tuesday he handed in his lab record two days early, every diagram labelled in blue ink. The teacher flipped through it and said, "Who helped you, Ujjwal?" That same afternoon he forgot his ID card, and the teacher said, loud enough for the whole row, "Of course. Some things never change." Vasudha, who sat next to him, saw him close the record slowly and stare at the desk. "Your diagrams were better than mine," she whispered. He shrugged. "Doesn't matter. I'm the lazy one." That evening he didn't start the next chapter.

qa.q: When did Ujjwal hand in his lab record?
qa.a: He handed it in two days early, on Tuesday.

qa.q: What does Ujjwal's "I'm the lazy one" suggest he is feeling?
qa.a: He feels defeated and hurt, as if the label has become who he is, so effort no longer seems worth it.

qa.q: How could a teacher support Ujjwal instead?
qa.a: The teacher could praise the early, careful lab record on its own merits and handle the ID card quietly, without tying both to an old label.

qa.q: How does Vasudha see Ujjwal's work?
qa.a: Vasudha sees it clearly as good, saying his diagrams were better than hers, and notices how the label is wearing him down.

grounding: Shows a teenager labelled lazy by a teacher whose early, careful work is doubted while a small slip is loudly noticed.

passage: Looking back at Class 9, I think one word did more damage than any mark. In the first week I forgot my homework twice, and Salma ma'am started calling me "careless Pankaj, our dreamy boy." After that it followed me everywhere. When I built a working water filter for the science fair, she asked which cousin had made it. When I scored the second-highest in the unit test, she said the paper must have been easy. But when I came in two minutes late after the bus broke down, it went into my diary for my parents to sign. By December I had stopped raising my hand. What was the point? Only in Class 10, with a new teacher who had never heard the word, did I start answering again. I was still the same boy.

qa.q: What did Pankaj build for the science fair?
qa.a: A working water filter.

qa.q: Why had Pankaj stopped raising his hand by December?
qa.a: He felt discouraged and unseen, because his good work was doubted while every small slip was recorded.

qa.q: What does the Class 10 change suggest a teacher could do?
qa.a: Come to each student fresh and judge the work in front of them, since without the label Pankaj started answering again.

qa.q: How might Salma ma'am have seen Pankaj's good test score?
qa.a: Through the careless label she read it as an easy paper rather than his effort, so the success didn't change her view.

grounding: A teenager looks back on being labelled careless by a teacher, so his real work was doubted while small slips were always recorded.

passage:
Class teacher's note, Class 9B

When I took over 9B this term, the previous teacher's handover note said: "Shankar: lazy. Doesn't try." I noticed the other teachers say the same thing about him in the staff room.

But in my first month, Shankar has submitted every science assignment on time. His diagram of the water cycle was the best in the class. When I mentioned it in the staff room, one teacher said, "He must have copied it."

When Shankar forgets his notebook, it's reported. When he answers well, nobody mentions it. I think the label has stuck so hard that people only see what fits it.

Today I asked Shankar how he feels in class. He shrugged and said, "Everyone thinks I'm lazy, so why try?"

I've shared his last month's work with the other teachers and asked them to notice his effort for two weeks.

Sarika

qa.q: What did the previous teacher's handover note say about Shankar?
qa.a: Shankar: lazy. Doesn't try.

qa.q: How does Shankar feel about the label?
qa.a: Shankar feels discouraged and hopeless, saying everyone thinks he's lazy so there is no point trying.

qa.q: What did Sarika do to help break the label?
qa.a: Sarika shared Shankar's actual work with other teachers and asked them to notice his effort for two weeks.

qa.q: How might the other teachers see Shankar after two weeks of noticing?
qa.a: They may start seeing his effort and good work that the label had hidden.

grounding: A teacher notes a teenager labelled lazy whose good work is ignored while every slip is noticed.

Mr Kulkarni called me "naughty Ojas" again today. It's been two years since I threw a paper plane in Class 7. Two years.

Today I finished my history project early and it was really good. I drew maps and everything. Mr Kulkarni looked at it for one second and said "Hmm." Then when I dropped my pencil box by accident, he said, "Ojas, always making trouble."

Leela told me after class that she thinks my project was the best. She said Mr Kulkarni didn't even read it properly.

I feel like whatever I do, he only sees the paper plane. Why bother being good?

Leela says I should show my project to the headmistress at the exhibition. Maybe. At least someone will look at it without the label.

Ojas
